data.title: RFK Jr. accepts PA child died of measles, says Shapiro hastily 'politicized' death
data.description:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. acknowledged Friday that measles caused the death of an infant in Pennsylvania, after previously questioning the state’s reporting of two measles-related deaths amid a growing outbreak.

Kennedy pointed to findings from Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, who confirmed Friday that the six-week-old child died from measles last month.

“The Lancaster County Coroner has now publicly stated that measles caused only the second infant’s death,” Kennedy wrote on social media.

The child was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic disorder that can lead to viral infections and typically results in death within months of birth.

In a post on social media, Kennedy fired back at Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) after he accused Kennedy of directing the Centers for Disease and Prevention (CDC) to not acknowledge the deaths in federal data.

“Instead of listening to the real doctors and public health experts, RFK chose to sow doubt, play politics, direct the CDC not to acknowledge these deaths, and even accuse me of fabricating these tragedies,” Shapiro wrote on the social platform X.

Kennedy had previously questioned whether the virus was the cause of the two deaths and asked that the cases reported by Pennsylvania’s health department be removed from the CDC’s national tally.

“The facts emerging now demonstrate why CDC waited for the evidence rather than allowing political grandstanding to dictate its reporting,” Kennedy wrote in a response Friday. “Governor Shapiro, by contrast, politicized these two tragic deaths before the underlying causes had been established.”

Pennsylvania health officials announced last week that two unvaccinated individuals had died in connection to the state’s measles outbreak, which has sickened 577 people and hospitalized 98.

The coroner drew a distinction between the two cases, which both involved infants.

In one case, a forensic pathologist determined the infant had died from a ruptured spleen and did not conclude that measles caused the death. In the second case, Diamantoni said a review of the 6-week-old infant’s medical records established that measles was the cause of death.

“The National Center for Health Statistics does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause but will update as it receives and reviews submitted records,” Kennedy said, adding that the CDC will continue to update its records as more information becomes available.

data.title: U.S. envoys arrive in Moscow to revive peace talks with Ukraine
data.description:
Two U.S. envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Moscow on Saturday as part of an effort to restart negotiations between Russia and Ukraine after a monthslong stall.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin authorized a 72-hour pause on strikes against Kyiv to facilitate the U.S. delegation’s visit to the country, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov. Their visit comes as Russia escalates the yearslong conflict with an increasing number of aerial attacks.

The two men touched down at Moscow’s governmental airport at 12:52 p.m. local time, state media TASS News Agency reported. Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, shared images on social media of him greeting Witkoff and Kushner as they exited the plane. 

Peskov told TASS the U.S. envoys will meet with Putin at the Kremlin later in the day. 

President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Friday the two men are “bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” though he did not elaborate on what the plan entailed.

Following their meeting with Russian officials, the U.S. envoys will travel to Kyiv on Sunday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. 

In a social media post on Saturday afternoon local time, Zelensky said he had “just spoken” with Witkoff and Kushner, confirming Ukraine’s military has also halted air strikes during their visit to both countries. 

The Ukrainian leader said in an earlier social media post that Russia hit two Ukrainian airports ahead of the U.S. envoys’ trip to the country. 

“From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process,” Zelensky wrote. “From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv.”

The yearslong dispute between Russia and Ukraine has intensified in recent weeks. Moscow has initiated near-continuous attacks in and around Kyiv for over a week, hitting buildings, warehouses and the central headquarters for the country’s security service. 

Ukraine has hit back with long-range attacks on oil storage and refining facilities in Russia.

In his Saturday statement, Zelensky expressed a commitment to having a “substantive conversation” with Kushner and Witkoff during their visit to Kyiv on Sunday. 

“On the diplomatic track, our actions must be, and will be, just as strong and effective – one hundred percent,” Zelensky wrote. “The plan for tomorrow’s diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the U.S. team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation.”

Witkoff and Kushner’s last known visit to Moscow was in January, before the US’s efforts to end the war in Ukraine slowed as the country entered its own military conflict with Iran. This weekend marks the pairs first time traveling to Kyiv for negotiations.

data.title: Judge rules former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can now be sued under NC 'homewrecker' law
data.description:
A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail.

Sinema has admitted to having a relationship with Matthew Ammel in 2024, but her attorneys have argued she cannot be sued in North Carolina because she has no ties to the state. 

U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon denied the former lawmaker’s request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the security guard’s ex-wife, Heather Ammel.

Sinema sent nine text messages to Matthew Ammel while he was at his North Carolina home, which Bragdon determined gives the state jurisdiction over the case. 

“These messages, considered together, show Ms. Sinema building and furthering a romantic relationship with Mr. Ammel—invading the marriage not just while he was away on trips with her but while he was home with his family in North Carolina,” the judge wrote in his order. 

North Carolina is one of the select states where people can sue for “alienation of affection,” which allows spouses to seek damages from the person responsible for breaking up their marriage. 

Heather Ammel sued the former senator at the end of last year, seeking at least $75,000 from Sinema. 

The former Sinema security guard’s ex-wife alleged she had “a good and loving marriage” prior to the former lawmaker’s interference. The couple separated on Nov. 1, 2024. 

She argued Sinema’s messages to her then-husband “exceeded the bounds of a normal working relationship and were of romantic and lascivious natures.”

The lawsuit also claimed the former lawmaker paid for Matthew Ammel’s psychedelic treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse and traumatic brain injuries resulting from his military deployments.

data.title: Family planning in the US should also support egg freezing
data.description:
Last month, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) brought a lot of attention to the plight of women who hope to have children later in life because they are at a point in their careers when they are not ready to be mothers, have not found a partner or, perhaps, because they are not ready financially or emotionally. 

Ocasio-Cortez is freezing her eggs and has posted about the experience on Instagram. She has been praised and criticized for sharing her experience. But whether one thinks it appropriate or not, her account demonstrates the importance of this option for many women who hope to have children at some point in the future.

It is an alternative more women are pursuing as they stay in school longer and wait later to start their families. Reproductive health research has consistently shown that as women age, it becomes harder for them to become pregnant and to carry a child to term. Egg freezing is an option that potentially allows women to have biological children at older ages.

Although Ocasio-Cortez enjoys many perks as a member of Congress, she is like most women in the U.S. when it comes to health insurance coverage and fertility. Her medical plan, provided through Congress, does not cover egg freezing, so she is paying out-of-pocket. By her account, she paid as much as $10,000.

The majority of women with private health insurance in the U.S. can relate — few have coverage of egg freezing. While any insurance company has the option to add provisions to their policies, it often takes a state mandate to get an insurance company to take on such a large increase in costs, and most states do not mandate that private health insurance carriers cover egg-freezing. When they do, it is often tied to a medical condition whose treatment reduces or halts a woman’s ovulation, such as chemotherapy or other highly invasive procedures. Elective egg freezing is not generally part of private health insurance coverage.

Given that, it should not surprise anyone to learn that low-income women have no support through public insurance either. Medicaid does not typically cover egg freezing, so Medicaid recipients who want to delay parenthood likely do not have that option. However, unlike Ocasio-Cortez, they do not have the financial resources to save for the process. Low-income women must either have children before they are ready to or forego the option to become a parent at all.

This demonstrates the asymmetry in family planning in the U.S. If a woman wants to avoid having children, contraceptive supplies and services are covered extensively in private health insurance policies. One can gain access to IUDs, oral contraceptives or any one of a number of birth control options at no or little cost. Low-income women also have complete coverage for contraceptive supplies and services through many publicly funded family planning programs, including Title X, which funds health care clinics for low-income women, or the Medicaid family planning program.

However, if a woman wants assistance in planning the timing of her childbearing, it is not available. This is but one-example of the lopsidedness of family planning in the U.S. Our programs are designed to assist when women want to restrict their childbearing but offer no support when women want to have children.

Much has been made of data that show that the number of births in the U.S. has been declining for decades. Some demographers project that our population will stop growing by the mid-2050s and then begin to shrink. Our Social Security program is already vulnerable to reductions in the number of young workers, but our demographic decline will affect our economic growth and military strength over time as well. 

The U.S. must start thinking more about policies that promote population growth in addition to policies that help women control their fertility. Both are necessary for a healthy family planning program. The U.S. is one of the few nations that does not recognize the importance of birth promotion as well as birth control in family planning. 

Leonard M. Lopoo is the Paul Volcker Chair in Behavioral Economics at Syracuse University’s Maxwell School. He is the author of the recently published book “Wanting Children: Family-Planning Policies and the Engineering of America’s Population.”

data.title: The fastest growing (and declining) job industries of the next decade: Federal data
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – While the health care industry is predicted to see the fastest job growth over the next decade, it’s not the only space where employment is expected to rise, new data from the Labor Department shows. Some aspects of the health care industry, meanwhile, may not see such growth. 

Last month, the Labor Department released data regarding its employment projections for the next decade. Through 2035, the report suggests the U.S. economy will add 5.9 million jobs. 

It’s the private healthcare and social assistance industry that is anticipated to add the most jobs of any sector, the Labor Department found. An entirely different industry is projected to have the fastest job growth, though: utilities. 

“The overall demand for electricity is expected to increase over the projections period due in large part to AI adoption and demand for related infrastructure, such as data centers,” the Labor Department said in the summary of its analysis. 

Which industries are growing?

Industries falling under health care and utilities comprise the top 10 projected to experience the fastest growth in wage and salary employment through 2035. 

Landing at the top of the rankings is solar electric power generation, which the Labor Department predicts will see a nearly 153% increase in employment over the next decade. That equates to about 26,000 jobs, a far cry from the increase of about 625,400 jobs projected for the services for the elderly and those with disabilities (more on this in a moment). 

You can view the top 10 fastest-growing industries below:

Among the industries above, the Labor Department projects the geothermal electric power generation sector will see employment increase by nearly 32%, or about 300 jobs. 

Though proportionally large for the industry, that’s a small increase in comparison to the industries projected to see the biggest employment growth in the coming years.

Services for the elderly and those with disabilities sit squarely at the top of that list:

While local government was able to rank among the top 10 above, other government workers may not fare as well in the coming decade.

Which industries could decline?

The apparel manufacturing sector, which employed 79,000 as of 2025, is forecast to diminish to 49,200 by 2035, a decline of about 30,000 jobs, or just shy of 38%. 

Projected to see an even greater decline is the printing and related support activities sector. Here, data suggests employment could drop by about 58,300 jobs, or 17%. 

The table below shows the 10 industries where the Labor Department has projected the most rapid decline in wage and salary employment through 2035. 

Though neither made it into the above rankings, the federal government and local elementary and secondary schools stand at the top of the list of industries that could see the largest decline in employment over the next decade.

The former, excluding the U.S. Postal Service, employed more than 2.3 million people in 2025, the Labor Department data shows. By 2035, it’s projected that will drop roughly 91,000 to about 2.2 million.

Local grade schools, meanwhile, employed more than 7.6 million last year. In the next decade, that is forecast to drop about 83,000 to more than 7.5 million.

Though the health care industry as a whole is projected to grow in the coming years, the Labor Department forecasts nursing facilities could see a notable dip of about 44,700 jobs.

The table below shows the 10 industries the Labor Department expects will see the greatest decline in employment by 2035:

While not reflected directly in the tables above, the Labor Department said office and administrative support occupations could be the most impacted of any due to the “growing adoption of AI.” The overall group may “shed 752,100 jobs” in the next 10 years, “the most of any major occupational group,” according to the report’s summary.

Changes in employment don’t necessarily signify people are losing their jobs. They could take up employment in a different industry, for example. 

The Labor Department also warns that it cannot “account for the inherent uncertainty of predicting long-term changes in the labor market.”

data.title: Pentagon gave polygraph tests to high-ranking officials to find leakers: Reports
data.description:
Some of the U.S. military’s highest-ranking officials were subject to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping Pentagon investigation into leaks to journalists on dwindling weapons stockpiles amid the Iran war, multiple reports suggest.

Military officials and civilian employees were tested in August, including roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the New York Times — which first reported the investigation Friday.

Several dozen other officials, including U.S. Central Command and other combatant commands, were also tested earlier this summer, CBS News reported.

Investigators reportedly questioned officials on whether they had disclosed classified information surrounding munitions shortages, including long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, to members of the press.

No one failed the questions, aimed to weed out anyone who may have leaked this information, two officials told CBS, adding that Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Dan Caine was not among those tested.

President Trump was furious over the disclosures, according to CBS, which reported that only a small number of people had access to the classified information. One official said investigators were also concerned about the possibility someone with high-level access could be working with foreign intelligence.

Polygraph exams are commonly conducted on officials with access to highly classified information. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security similarly used the devices to determine the source of press leaks.

But in this case, current and former officials reportedly describe the number of senior military personnel tested in the investigation as extraordinary.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told CBS the department “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”

The investigation follows months of reporting about the rate at which the U.S. has used some of its most advanced weapons since the war with Iran began on Feb. 28.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has pushed back on reports of shortages, while President Trump publicly laid out his anger over leaks within the department.

“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” the president wrote in an August Truth Social post. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”

data.title: US launches retaliatory strikes on 3 Iranian oil carriers in response to attacks against Navy warships
data.description:
U.S. Central Command (Centcom) on Saturday conducted strikes on several Iranian crude oil carriers in response to “multiple unprovoked” Iranian attacks on two U.S. Navy warships, according to the military command. 

The U.S. military “permanently disabled” three of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) crude oil carriers located near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman. No U.S. service members were harmed during the Iranian attacks, according to Centcom.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours,” Centcom Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement shared on social media. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.” 

The exchange of hostilities follows escalating military operations from both sides this week. After the U.S. carried out roughly 100 strikes against Iranian targets on Tuesday, Tehran responded by targeting U.S. military bases and allies in strikes across the Middle East.

Vice President JD Vance waived off concerns about the state of the conflict during a Thursday press briefing, telling reporters he “wouldn’t call it a war.”

“Right now, there is no active shooting,” he continued. “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up.”

President Trump and his administration have repeatedly pushed back on public criticism of this conflict, which has now stretched into a sixth month. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has placed a strain on the global energy supply, raising fuel and other costs for U.S. consumers. 

“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday.

data.title: When '12 Angry Men' becomes one angry man
data.description:
“I hope that guy can sleep well at night.”

Those words from Kevin Reddington on the steps of the Plymouth, Massachusetts Courthouse were part of a diatribe against the “guy” who was reportedly the sole holdout in the Lindsay Clancy trial. The scene was a fitting end to a visceral trial, but it added a vindictive element that should prompt Judge William Sullivan to call out the seasoned defense attorney.

After declaring that the 11-1 mistrial was “no time to gloat,” Reddington bragged repeatedly about “crushing” District Attorney Tim Cruz, whom he also attacked. He insisted that, in the trial, no one said a single negative thing about his client as a mother — ignoring that little matter of the three young children whom she had strangled to death, one by one.

But it was his attack on the holdout juror that was a breathtaking abandonment of restraint and decency. Reddington knows it is very likely that the name of this juror (he has already been identified as one of only three males on the jury) will eventually be uncovered by Internet sleuths. He effectively put a target on the back of a juror who committed the unpardonable sin of not being convinced by his arguments.

The fact that this is one of the three male jurors only ramped up the rage. This case prompted a striking gender divide between men and women, with many women expressing sympathy for Clancy and anger at the system for failing her. 

For Reddington and many viewers, the hung jury was less “Twelve Angry Men” and more like “One Angry Man.” Indeed, in addition to attacking the juror, women outside of the courthouse heckled Cruz as he tried to speak to the press, shouting that he “only cares about the three children. What about the Mom?”

Reddington followed up by saying that Cruz really did not care about the children (because he looked down to read their names). He also accused the holdout jurors of wasting the time of the jury, complaining “that guy stole seven weeks from those jurors.” 

It was an ironic twist on the 1957 classic. In that movie, Juror number eight (Ford) was repeatedly attacked for “wasting time” and not yielding to the majority — until he ultimately convinced all of his peers.

Earlier in the day, Reddington had asked a Massachusetts Supreme Court justice for an emergency order to force Sullivan not to declare a mistrial, and instead to remove the holdout in favor of an alternate. It was an utterly meritless effort, but Reddington used the filing to further denounce the juror. He compared the juror’s refusal to vote for his client as akin to leaving a racist on a jury. In this case, he suggested that the “guy” was a virtual anti-disability version of “Bull” Connor or some deranged “ableist.”

The rising hatred toward this juror reflects how an act deemed noble in one context can be denounced as craven in another.

Take the 1957 classic movie. Viewers love to watch Henry Ford stand alone against his fellow jurors to raise reasonable doubt in favor of the young defendant. But in this version, the sole juror believed that his fellow jurors were ignoring the defendant’s culpability.

Imagine the movie’s outcome if Reddington’s approach had been accepted in 1957, where Ford could be pulled into court, questioned about his intransigence, and ultimately replaced with an alternate in order to flip the vote.

For all of the anger it has generated, the Clancy trial shows the best of our justice system. We have a system in which a single juror can stand against not only the rest of the jury, but against the world. The trial showed zealous counsel on both sides and a conscientious judge who ensured a fair trial despite the powerful emotions in society.

You can disagree with this juror and the outcome but still celebrate that our legal system comes down not to judges or lawyers, but to simple citizens doing justice in thousands of cases a year. It comes down to whether every juror can vote not for a popular choice, but for a moral one. 

That is why some of us were so shocked by Reddington’s public attack on this one juror. This is not who we are supposed to be as officers of the court. We stand in the path of the mob, not leading it. In another great movie, “To Kill a Mockingbird,” Gregory Peck captured that role from the novel most vividly as Atticus Finch, standing before a jail to stop a lynch mob. 

Finch showed that the strength of any legal system is ultimately only as strong as each individual’s ability to stand alone. He tells his daughter Scout, “The one thing that doesn’t abide by majority rule is a person’s conscience.”

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.“

data.title: See the best public universities for 2027, according to Niche
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – While the cost of an education may not be getting any cheaper, a new analysis released Tuesday seeks to help school shoppers identify the top public universities for 2027.

Niche, an education research platform, published the results as part of its annual set of nationwide school rankings.

“Public universities are an engine for social mobility. They give students access to great academic programs and research opportunities, often at a more affordable cost than private institutions,” said Allison Shrivastava, economist at Niche, told Nexstar in an email. “Year after year, the top-ranked publics show just how much opportunity these institutions have to offer students from many backgrounds and ZIP codes.”

The top school in the ranking, according to Niche’s analysis, is the University of California at Los Angeles, in Los Angeles. The large public university has an acceptance rate of 9%, Niche found, and roughly 33,470 undergraduate students. The school boasts a graduation rate of 93%, and the top areas of study are economics, political science and government, and psychology.

“The schools at the top of this year’s Top Public Universities list are some of the biggest names in higher education, but they aren’t interchangeable,” Shirvasta said. “Each offers a different mix of academics, values, and campus experience. That’s exactly what our rankings are designed to surface so that students can build their college list with confidence.”

See the top 25 public universities, according to Niche, below:

See the complete list on the Niche website.

The new ranking comes amid recent reports of ballooning student loan default numbers.

Across the country, the number of borrowers with defaulted student loans jumped by more than 4.2 million from April 2025 to March 2026, according to an Associated Press analysis. The surge includes many who went off track in 2024, when loan payments started coming due again after a pandemic-era freeze.

Hundreds of thousands more are months behind on payments, and another surge in defaults could be on the way. Millions of borrowers are facing higher monthly payments as the government dismantles its most affordable income-driven repayment option, the SAVE plan, one of several changes the Education Department says are intended to simplify a fragmented system.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: US only country to oppose UN resolution correcting Africa's size on world maps
data.description:
The U.S. was the only country to not support a United Nations resolution adjusting the appearance of Africa and other regions on world maps. 

The body passed the “Correct the Map” initiative by a margin of 164 to one, with six nations abstaining from the vote. 

The resolution, which was introduced by the West African country Togo, does not require the abandonment of the long-used Mercator projection. It instead encourages the use of equal-area projections that more accurately depict relative country sizes. 

Yaryna Ferencevych, the deputy U.S. representative to the U.N. Economic and Social Council, said in a statement explaining the U.S.’s vote that this measure, “mocks the work and purpose of this institution.”

“Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th century, and their role in promoting reparations and ‘cognitive justice,’” she said. 

“Resolutions like this and the ideological agenda they promote, are barnacles on our work here, and the reason this institution is losing its credibility,” Ferencevych continued. “When the United Nations questions why it is losing legitimacy in the world, and is not taken seriously, time and again, we point to resolutions such as this.” 

The “Correct the Map” campaign has encouraged nations around the world to adopt the Equal Earth projection, which was designed by cartographers in 2018 to present a more proportionally accurate depiction of the world.

The African Union Commission said the initiative “marks a historic step toward accurate and equitable global cartographic representation.” 

“For centuries, the Mercator projection distorted global geography, shrinking Africa to the size of Greenland when our continent is actually 14 times larger,” the group wrote on social media.

“Today’s resolution promotes equal-area maps like Equal Earth across classrooms, media, and international institutions ensuring the world map finally reflects Africa’s true scale, weight, and place in the world.”
